spotlight.title: Spotlight: Ormson Supply Co.
spotlight.dek: Mid-century furniture, records and a taxidermied deer in the window, on KK since 2020
spotlight.body:
Ormson Supply Co. is a vintage shop at 2866 S. Kinnickinnic Ave., on the corner storefront with the big plate-glass windows (and, often, a taxidermied deer standing guard). It sells mid-century modern furniture, much of it Scandinavian, along with records, clothing, housewares and whatever else the owners think is worth hauling home.

The business started as Brew City Salvage, which owner Caleb Nickel ran out of his home before opening storefronts in Waukesha and then on National Avenue in Walker's Point. Nickel, a former truck driver who also ran a window-cleaning business, told the Shepherd Express that rummaging with his mom as a kid is "ingrained in my DNA." His cousin Ross Severson, a mixed-media artist who runs the vintage housewares collection 414 Modern, became his business partner.

In September 2020 the shop moved to Bay View, a move Nickel told Urban Milwaukee he had wanted for years, and took a new name. Ormson is a family name: both cousins' mothers were Ormsons, and the Norwegian roots suit a store heavy on Scandinavian pieces. The black-and-white logo is the family's bumerke, an old Norwegian mark once used to label property. Nickel also said the old name kept bringing in calls from people hunting for car parts.

What you'll find changes constantly, because the owners are out sourcing pieces most days of the week. Nickel has said he's partial to handmade furniture over mass-produced pieces, and the shop has held monthly weekend "Small Sales" on smaller items. Customers can also ask about pieces they see on the shop's Facebook and Instagram pages.

This week the shop posted a video tour of new stock and said it will be open 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Small Business Saturday, with a nudge to support small shops, many of which it says need the help this year.

Ormson Supply Co., 2866 S. Kinnickinnic Ave. Open Saturday, Nov. 28, 11 a.m.-4 p.m.; check its Facebook or Instagram (@ormsonsupply) for other hours.

buzz.headline: Yes, there really is an 1891 lightship buried under Cupertino Park
buzz.body: A r/milwaukee thread this week revived one of Bay View's best yarns: a ship sits under the lakefront park. It's true. Lightship No. 57, built in Toledo in 1891, ended up at South Shore in 1928, when a club of young Bay View men called the Unknowns bought the hulk as a clubhouse, and it was later buried under fill, according to the Wisconsin Marine Historical Society. Its remains have been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1996.

history.title: Bay View Bowl: one of Milwaukee's 200 bowling alleys, still rolling
history.text: A building permit from October 1924 started the bowling alley on KK. A century later, Bay View Bowl is one of the few of Milwaukee's old neighborhood lanes still open.
history.body:
Bay View Bowl almost started life as a movie theater. In 1915 a developer took out a permit to build an 800-seat "moving picture" house on Kinnickinnic Avenue, but it was never built, according to Urban Milwaukee's history of the building.

In October 1924, Badger Building Services took out a permit for three stores, two flats and bowling alleys on the lot, and the alleys went up first since they needed no basement. The current owners date the building to 1925, which is why they threw a 90th birthday party in 2015 with 90-cent games and shoes.

Bowling was big business then: Milwaukee once had some 200 alleys, most of them busy with leagues. Through the decades the KK building held a barbershop, an ice cream parlor during Prohibition, a tavern and dance hall afterward, a beauty shop and a diner, while the bowling carried on in back. It ran as Bay View Recreation Parlor and later Roghan Recreation, and around 1970 an operator named Martin Alivo gave it the name Bay View Bowl and the Lannon stone front it still wears.

Today fewer than 20 of the city's old alleys remain. Bay View Bowl still has wooden lanes, and in recent years it has added glow bowling and local art on the walls, and it's one of the neighborhood's most familiar signs at 2416 S. Kinnickinnic Ave.
